lead: Two processes, each holding one resource and each waiting for the other's, will wait forever. That state is a deadlock, and you cannot see it by looking at one process — it is a property of a set of processes and the resources between them. Deadlocks appear in database transactions, file locks, device drivers and thread pools that grab two mutexes in the wrong order. This chapter builds the system model, draws the resource-allocation graph, and states the four conditions that must all be true at once before a deadlock can exist.
prereq: You need: process states from Unit 2, and the shared-resource conflict of 3.1.

sections.h3: Resource types, instances and the resource-allocation graph

blocks.text: A resource type R is a class of identical things a process may need: printers, disk drives, memory blocks, files, semaphores, mutex locks. Each type has a fixed number of instances W. A lab with two identical printers has one resource type R with W = 2; two printers on different networks are two types.
A process uses a resource in a fixed sequence.

items: Request: ask for an instance. If none is free, the process blocks.
Allocate: the OS gives one instance to the process.
Use: the process works with the resource.
Release: the process returns the instance.

blocks.text: The resource-allocation graph (RAG) is a directed graph recording the current state of all this. Nodes are of two kinds: a circle for each process P1 … Pn, and a box for each resource type R1 … Rm with W dots inside, one dot per instance. Edges mean holdings and waits.

items: Request edge P → R: process P is waiting for an instance of R.
Assignment edge R → P: one instance of R is held by P.
Total edges = pending requests + current holdings.

A box has one dot per instance, always, held or free. When an instance is held, the assignment edge starts at that dot and goes to the process; a dot with no outgoing assignment edge is free. Three printers with two held still show three dots, with two assignment edges leaving two of them.

blocks.text: A process can hold several resources and wait for several at once, so one node may have many edges in and out. The graph is a snapshot; it changes with every request and release.

sections.h3: Deadlock, starvation and the four necessary conditions

blocks.text: Deadlock: a set of processes is blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another member of the set, so none can ever release anything. Starvation (indefinite postponement) is different: a process waits a long time while others keep taking the resource, but the resource is still being released and could reach it. A deadlocked process is also starving; a starving process is not necessarily deadlocked.

In a priority scheduler with a steady stream of high-priority arrivals, a low-priority job may starve for hours while the CPU is never idle — unfair, but no deadlock. A deadlock needs a closed loop: process A holds lock L1 and waits for L2, process B holds L2 and waits for L1. Neither can proceed and neither will release, so the wait truly never ends.
Four conditions, listed by Coffman and co-authors in 1971, must all hold together for a deadlock to exist. If any one is false, deadlock is impossible.

items: Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-shareable, so one instance serves one process at a time. A read-only file breaks this.
Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while requesting another.
No preemption: a resource is released only voluntarily by its holder; the OS cannot snatch it back.
Circular wait: a closed chain of waits exists.

blocks.text: {P0, P1, …, Pn} : P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 waits for one held by P2, …, Pn waits for one held by P0
blocks.where: the P's are distinct processes and n ≥ 0; the chain must close on itself. A line of waits that ends at a free resource is not circular wait.

sections.h3: Cycles: always necessary, sufficient only for single instances

blocks.text: Look at the RAG. If it has no cycle, no process waits in a closed loop, so no deadlock exists: a cycle is necessary. It is sufficient only when every resource in the cycle has exactly one instance. Then the cycle is the deadlock, and every process on it is blocked forever.

Give R1 and R2 two instances each. P1 holds one R1 and requests one R2. P2 holds one R2 and requests one R1. P3 holds one R2. The graph contains the cycle P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1, yet R1 has a free instance, so P2's request is granted; P2 finishes, releases both, then P1 runs. No deadlock. With several instances a cycle is only a warning; you must test whether free instances can break it, which is what detection in 3.8 does.

Threads deadlock the same way with locks, and a mutex is a single-instance resource, so there a cycle is a real deadlock. Thread A locks m1 then m2; thread B locks m2 then m1. If each takes its first lock before either takes its second, A waits for m2 held by B and B waits for m1 held by A. Mutex locks are from 3.3.
Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock: that is prevention, in 3.6. Granting only requests that leave a safe state is avoidance, in 3.7.

figure.caption: Each resource has one instance and both are held, so each process waits for the one the other holds. The four edges close one cycle and 0 processes can finish: deadlock.

spec.aria: A square resource-allocation graph: P1 holds R1 and wants R2, P2 holds R2 and wants R1, with the four edges forming a cycle.

examples.question: A system has two resource types, R1 and R2, with one instance each. Process P1 holds R1 and requests an instance of R2. Process P2 holds R2 and requests an instance of R1. (a) Draw the resource-allocation graph. (b) Count the request edges, the assignment edges and the total edges. (c) Is the system deadlocked? How many processes can finish?
steps: Step 1 — nodes: circles P1 and P2, boxes R1 and R2, each box with one dot because each type has 1 instance.
Step 2 — P1 holds R1, so draw the assignment edge R1 → P1. P1 wants R2, so draw the request edge P1 → R2.
Step 3 — P2 holds R2, so draw the assignment edge R2 → P2. P2 wants R1, so draw the request edge P2 → R1.
Step 4 — count: request edges = 2 (P1 → R2, P2 → R1). Assignment edges = 2 (R1 → P1, R2 → P2). Total edges = 2 + 2 = 4.
Step 5 — follow the arrows: P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1. The chain closes, so there is one cycle, of length 4 edges.
Step 6 — R1 has 1 instance and it is held by P1; R2 has 1 instance and it is held by P2. Free instances = 0, so neither request can be granted.
Step 7 — P1 cannot get R2, P2 cannot get R1, neither releases anything. Processes that can finish = 0.
examples.answer: The graph has 4 edges (2 request, 2 assignment) forming one cycle; with 1 instance per resource and 0 free instances no process can complete, so the system is deadlocked and 0 processes finish.

assign_edges = 2
total = request_edges + assign_edges
finished = 0
print(total)

traps: A cycle in the resource-allocation graph is not always a deadlock. With several instances per resource the cycle can clear itself; only single-instance resources make a cycle equal to a deadlock.
Hold and wait is not circular wait. P1 holding R1 while waiting for R2, and P2 holding R2 while waiting for R3, is a chain that ends at free R3 — no deadlock.
The four conditions are necessary, not sufficient. A system can satisfy all four and still run forever without deadlock if requests never close a loop.
No preemption is about the resource, not the CPU. Swapping a process out does not take back its file lock, so preempting the CPU does not break this condition.

Starvation is not deadlock. A starved process would finish once the resource reached it. A deadlocked process waits in a closed loop, so waiting longer never helps, though adding an extra instance of the contended resource type can sometimes break the cycle.

quiz.q: State the four necessary conditions for deadlock.
quiz.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait — all four must hold at the same time.

quiz.q: What does one dot inside a resource box of a resource-allocation graph represent?
quiz.a: One dot is one instance of that resource type. Whether an instance is free or held is shown by the edges: if an assignment edge leaves a dot, that instance is held by the process it points to; a dot with no outgoing assignment edge is free.

quiz.q: Why is a cycle in the resource-allocation graph necessary but not sufficient for deadlock?
quiz.a: No cycle means no closed chain of waits, so no deadlock. With several instances per type, a free instance can satisfy a request on the cycle, so the cycle can break.

quiz.q: Give one example of starvation without deadlock and one of deadlock.
quiz.a: Starvation: a low-priority job never scheduled while higher-priority jobs keep arriving. Deadlock: two threads, each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's.

quiz.q: R1 has 2 instances and R2 has 2 instances. P1 holds one R1 and requests R2. P2 holds one R2 and requests R1. P3 holds one R2. Is there a cycle? Is the system deadlocked?
quiz.a: Cycle P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1 exists. R1 still has 1 free instance, so P2's request is granted; P2 finishes and releases R2, then P1 runs. No deadlock.

quiz.q: Two threads take locks m1 and m2, one in the order m1 then m2 and the other in the order m2 then m1. Which of the four conditions does a global lock-ordering rule remove, and why?
quiz.a: Circular wait. If every thread takes locks in one fixed order, say by address, a thread can only wait for a lock of higher order, so a wait chain cannot close on itself. Mutual exclusion and hold and wait remain.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production kernels ship deadlock detectors: Linux's lockdep watches lock ordering at run time and reports a cycle before the machine hangs, and database engines keep a wait-for graph and abort a transaction when a cycle appears. Rust's ownership rules rule out data races at compile time, but a lock-ordering deadlock between two threads still compiles and hangs at run time, so lock ordering is still the programmer's job. Search for lockdep, wait-for graph and lock ordering to go deeper.
